newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: GOLDEN WEST SAYS CAN HANDLE MINE CLOSURES.
newsitem.headline: GOLDEN WEST SAYS CAN HANDLE MINE CLOSURES.

text.p: Precious metals refiner Golden West Refining Corp Ltd said on Tuesday it was in a good position to withstand mine closures due to recent falls in gold prices.
The company also said it aimed to pay its first dividend at the end of 1997/98 (April/March) at a proposed payout ratio of of about 20 percent of after-tax earnings.
Golden West last year showed a 15 precent increase in annual net profit to A$1.18 million.

"In light of the recent events in the gold market, the company's decision to diversify its earnings base away from its historical core would appear timely," chairman Richard Lee told the annual meeting.

Gold prices slipped to their lowest level in about 12 years last month after the Reserve Bank of Australia said it had sold 167 tonnes of bullion reserves in favour of foreign currency backed securities.
The fall in prices threatens to make some mines uneconomical as cash operating costs at a growing number of deposits begin to exceed market prices and forward hedge positions expire.
Prices have since recovered somewhat, although analysts say the long-term direction for prices remains uncertain.
Golden West manages operations in Australia, Papua New Guinea, Canada and the United States with combined annual refining capacity of nine million ounces of gold and 55 million ounces of silver.

"Since its inception, the Australian business has been built upon the growth of primary gold production, the objective being to fill the refinery with a feedstock of gold and silver dore from mines in the region," managing director Mike Ryan said.

However, in the United States, where Golden West last year paid US$9 million to acquire precious metals refiner Handy and Harman Refining Group, only 15 percent of earnings came from refining gold and silver derived from mine production, he said.

Other sources of revenue in the United States are derived from a range of industrial and recycled segments. These include recovery of silver from photographic waste and recovery of gold, silver, platinum and palladium from discrete devices and printed circuit boards form old electronic equipment.
Diversity has brought exposure to a broader range of markets, Ryan told the meeting.
"In the first quarter, we have seen extreme volatility in the platinum group metals, with a doubling of the palladium price and large increases in the cost of leasing these metals."
In the short-term, these developments would impact on operating costs but in the medium term they should lead to opportunities to improve earnings, Ryan said.
Also, while lower gold and silver prices impact earnings, increased demand generated by lower prices would create opportunities later in the year, he said.
